name: fastcpp::algo::sort / radix_sort (developer source)
workload: Sort 1M int64 elements across seven input patterns (random, already-sorted, reverse-sorted, almost-sorted with 1% swapped, few-unique/8 values, sawtooth, sorted+1% appended random), gcc 13.3.0 -O3 -march=native -std=c++23; separately, LSD radix_sort vs std::sort on random uint64 from n=64 to n=4,194,304.
claimed_speedup: vs std::sort on 1M int64: 6.63x already-sorted, 3.42x few-unique, 2.33x sorted+1% appended, 2.28x random, 1.71x sawtooth, 1.55x reverse-sorted; LOSES 0.93x on almost-sorted (1% positions swapped), where std::sort wins by 7-10% consistently. A pivot-arrangement fix (median placed directly at *first vs swapped in afterward) is separately worth 2.86x on reverse-sorted input (3.803ms vs 10.864ms). radix_sort vs std::sort: peak 4.30x at n=16,384, falls to 2.06x at n=4M (where fastcpp::algo::sort itself is faster than radix_sort: 140.5ms vs 158.2ms), and LOSES at small n (0.92x at n=1024 crossover, 0.23x at n=64).
compiler_and_flags: gcc 13.3.0, -O3 -march=native -std=c++23 (benchmarks force -O3 via fastcpp_bench_opt in root CMakeLists; run label 2026-09-04-algorithms)
hardware: Intel Xeon @ 2.10GHz, 4 cores (SSE4.2, AVX2, BMI2, AVX-512F/VL, PCLMULQDQ), Ubuntu 24.04, Linux 6.18, shared cloud VM
tradeoffs: Pattern-defeating quicksort loses to std::sort by ~7-10% on almost-sorted data (1% of positions swapped): the bounded sorted-run probe (at most 8 moves per side) fails once displacement exceeds that budget, so the wasted probe is pure overhead; wins on the other six tested patterns. radix_sort needs O(n) scratch memory, supports no custom comparator, and only works on key types decomposable into bytes; its advantage window is roughly n=1024..1M, and past ~4M it is slower than the project's own comparison sort.
caveats: Developer source is a PRIVATE repo (private:developer-source, 0 stars, 0 forks), readable only via authenticated `gh api`. Per orchestrator instruction, private code is not 'public' so this is capped below tier A even though compiler, flags, and CPU model are all fully stated in results/fastest.json's run metadata (verified against bench/bench_sort.cpp and the sort.hpp/radix_sort.hpp headers). Only libstdc++/gcc tested; no libc++ or MSVC STL comparison. First-party benchmark authored by the same project, not independently reproduced. The repo's own results file states absolute times are not comparable across differently-timed runs on this shared cloud VM; only within-row ratios are treated as meaningful, which is what is reported here.

name: fastcpp::algo::lower_bound (branchless / Eytzinger) (developer source)
workload: Lower-bound search over sorted int arrays: 4096 ints (16 KiB, L1-resident) and 4.2M ints (16 MiB, exceeds L2), comparing a branchless-cmov lower_bound, a prefetching variant, and an Eytzinger (breadth-first) layout against std::lower_bound, gcc 13.3.0 -O2 -march=native.
claimed_speedup: 5.83x on the L1-resident array (branchless cmov: 11.562ns vs std::lower_bound's 67.401ns, 4096 ints). 1.91x on the DRAM-sized array (explicit-prefetch variant: 224.04ns vs std::lower_bound's 427.706ns, 4.2M ints). Eytzinger layout measured 80.132ns on that same 4.2M-int DRAM workload, i.e. 5.34x vs std::lower_bound's 427.706ns (derived from page data: the Eytzinger row's own recorded baseline is 'branchless cmov, sorted layout' at 317.093ns, a 3.96x win, not std::lower_bound directly, but both rows share the same run and workload size).
hardware: Intel Xeon @ 2.10GHz (AVX2, SSE4.2, BMI2), 4 cores, Ubuntu 24.04, Linux 6.18, shared cloud VM
tradeoffs: Plain branchless search (no prefetch) is UNSTABLE on DRAM-sized data: across five runs it measured 0.72x-1.49x of std::lower_bound, i.e. no reliable win, because going branchless discards the free prefetch a mispredicted branch would otherwise give the wrong-path cache line; only the explicit-prefetch variant is a stable win when memory-bound. Eytzinger layout requires a build/reorder step, leaves the array unsorted (build-once/search-many only), and merely ties plain branchless on cache-resident (16 KiB) arrays. The exact C++ spelling of the branchless step decides whether gcc emits cmov or a branch (`base += size_t(cond) * half` vs a ternary) -- verified by disassembly, not portable across compilers/versions per the source comments.
caveats: Developer source is a PRIVATE repo, readable only via authenticated `gh api`; per orchestrator instruction this is capped below tier A despite full compiler/flags/CPU disclosure in results/fastest.json (cross-checked against include/fastcpp/algo/binary_search.hpp, which documents the same cmov-vs-branch finding). Only libstdc++/gcc tested; no libc++ or MSVC STL run. First-party benchmark, not independently reproduced. The Eytzinger-vs-std::lower_bound figure is a cross-row derived ratio (both rows share run 2026-09-02-core and the identical 4.2M-int workload), not a number printed directly against std::lower_bound in the Eytzinger row itself.
